source_text:
Quid faciam cum errore peruersis et consuetudine inplicatis miserrimis animis? non enim sciunt isti homines. quid loquantur, cum haec loquuntur; non enim adtendunt. rogo, nemo uos urget, nemo in certamen premit, nemo praeteritis insultat erroribus, nisi qui diuinam misericordiam expertus non est. ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur. intuemini paululum sine animositate et amaritudine — omnes homines sumus, non nos, sed errores et falsitates oderimus — quaeso, intuemini paululum. deus misericordiarum, adiuua intuentes et uerum quaerentibus interius lumen accende. quid enim intellegimus, si non intellegimus rectum melius esse quam prauum? quaero ergo a uobis, si placide modesteque accipitis, rectum latus terrae tenebrarum, quod recto lateri terrae lucis adiungitur, si quispiam deprauaret, nullamne illi pulchritudinem adimeret. necesse est fateamini, si latrare nolitis, non solum ei, si deprauetur, pulchritudinem auferri, sed eam etiam pulchritudinem, quam cum recto latere terrae luminis potuit habere communem. hanc ergo auferens et de recto prauum faciens, ut discordaret, quod concordabat, et abhorreret, quod congruebat, numquid aliquam inde auferret substantiam? sic ergo discite non substantiam malum esse, sed sicut in corpore conmutatione formae in deterius amitti speciem uel potius minui et foedum dici, quod pulchrum antea dicebatur, et displicere corpus, quod ante placuerat: sic in animo rectae uoluntatis decus, quo pie iusteque uiuitur, conmutata in deterius uoluntate deprauari; quo peccato effici animam miseram, quae honestate rectae uoluntatis beatitatem obtinebat, nulla addita detractaue substantia.
Deinde etiam illud cogitate, quia etsi concedamus aliis causis latus terrae tenebrarum malum esse, quod obscurum, quod tenebrosum uel si quid aliud dici potest, non tamen in eo, quod rectum est, malum est. sicut ergo concedo esse in eius colore aliquid mali, sic necesse est et uos concedatis esse in eius rectitudine aliquid boni. nefas est itaque hoc quantumcumque boni est alienare ab artifice deo, a quo esse omne bonum, quod in quacumque natura est, nisi credimus, perniciosissime erramus. quomodo ergo ille et summum malum esse dicit hanc terram, in cuius lateris rectitudine inuenio, quantum ad corpus adtinet, non paruae pulchritudinis bonum, et ab omnipotente atque optimo deo eam uult esse penitus alienam, cum id ipsum bonum, quod in illa inuenimus, cui alii tribuendum sit nisi auctori bonorum omnium. non inueniamus? sed malum erat, inquit, etiam illud latus. puta malum esse: deterius esset certe, si non rectum, sed distortum esset. quomodo est igitur summum malum, quo potest aliquid cogitari deterius ? deinde necesse est aliquid boni sit. quo carendo fit res quaecumque deterior; carendo autem rectitudine fieret latus illud deterius: inest ergo illi boni aliquid, rectitudo. et numquam mihi dices, unde inest, nisi ad eum te contuleris. a quo siue magna siue parua, omnia tamen bona esse fateamur. sed iam a lateris huius consideratione transeamus ad alia.
thought_title: Rectitude as a good in the land of darkness
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, asking them to consider whether the straight side of the land of darkness contains a good that cannot be attributed to the supreme evil.
pass_a_gloss: What shall I do with most wretched souls, perverted by error and entangled by habit? For these men do not know what they are saying, when they say these things; for they do not pay attention. I ask, no one urges you, no one presses you into a contest, no one insults past errors, except the one who has not experienced divine mercy. So that he might be free from errors, let us only work at this, that they may at some time be ended. Look for a little while without animosity and bitterness — we are all human, let us hate not ourselves, but errors and falsehoods — I beg, look for a little while. God of mercies, help those who look, and kindle the inner light for those seeking the truth. For what do we understand, if we do not understand that the straight is better than the crooked? Therefore I ask you, if you receive it calmly and modestly, if anyone should make crooked the straight side of the land of darkness, which is joined to the straight side of the land of light, would he take away no beauty from it? You must confess, if you do not wish to bark, that not only is beauty taken away from it, if it is made crooked, but also that beauty which it could have had in common with the straight side of the land of light. Therefore the one who takes this away and makes the straight crooked, so that it would be discordant, which was concordant, and would shrink from, which was in agreement, would he take away any substance from it? Therefore learn in this way that evil is not substance, but just as in a body, by the change of form for the worse, the form is lost or rather diminished, and that is called ugly which was previously called beautiful, and the body displeases which previously had pleased: so in the soul the honor of right will, by which one lives piously and justly, is made crooked when the will is changed for the worse; by which sin the soul is made wretched, which held blessedness by the honorableness of right will, with no substance added or taken away. Then also consider this, because even if we grant that for other reasons the side of the land of darkness is evil, because it is dark, because it is shadowy, or if anything else can be said, nevertheless in that which is straight, it is not evil. Therefore just as I grant that there is something of evil in its color, so it is necessary that you also grant that there is something of good in its straightness. Therefore it is wicked to alienate this, however much of good it is, from God the artificer, from whom every good that is in any nature exists, unless we believe this, we err most destructively. How then does he say that this land is the supreme evil, in the straightness of whose side I find, as far as pertains to body, a good of not small beauty, and he wishes it to be utterly alien from the omnipotent and best God, when this very good, which we find in it, to whom else should it be attributed except to the author of all goods, we would not find? But that side was evil, he says. Suppose it was evil: it would certainly be worse, if it were not straight, but distorted. How then is it the supreme evil, than which something worse can be thought? Then it is necessary that there be something of good, by the lack of which any thing becomes worse; but by the lack of straightness that side would become worse: therefore something of good is in it, straightness. And you will never tell me whence it is in it, unless you have taken yourself to him, from whom, whether great or small, let us confess that all goods nevertheless exist. But let us now pass from the consideration of this side to other things.

choices.english: the straight side of the land of darkness
choices.why: Keeps the literal spatial language of Mani's myth, which Augustine is analyzing; 'straight' preserves the geometric sense of 'rectum' that Augustine contrasts with 'prauum' (crooked).
rejected: the right side of the land of darkness
the correct side of the land of darkness

choices.why: The verb 'deprauare' means to distort or make crooked, and Augustine is playing on the contrast between 'rectum' (straight) and 'prauum' (crooked); 'make crooked' preserves this physical sense.
The glossary specifies 'form' for 'species', and Augustine is using it in the sense of the beauty or form of a thing that is lost in corruption.
'Artifex' means craftsman or maker; 'artificer' preserves the sense of God as the maker of all goods, which is central to Augustine's argument that every good comes from God.
The glossary specifies 'supreme evil' for 'summum malum', and Augustine is arguing that the land of darkness cannot be the supreme evil because it contains goods.
The verb 'latrare' literally means to bark like a dog; Augustine uses it to describe the Manichaeans' refusal to concede the point, and the literal rendering preserves the vividness of his rhetoric.

pass_b_english: What am I to do with souls so miserably entangled in perverse error and habit? These people do not know what they are saying when they say these things; they do not pay attention. I ask you, no one is forcing you, no one is pressing you into a contest, no one is mocking your past errors—except the one who has not experienced God's mercy. To be rid of errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end. Look at this for a little while without hostility and bitterness—we are all human; let us hate not ourselves but errors and falsehoods—please, look at it for a little while. God of mercies, help those who look, and kindle an inner light for those who seek the truth. For what do we understand, if we do not understand that straight is better than crooked?

So I ask you, if you will receive this calmly and modestly: if someone were to make crooked the straight side of the land of darkness, which is joined to the straight side of the land of light, would he not take away some of its beauty? You must admit—unless you want to bark—that not only is its beauty taken away if it is made crooked, but also the beauty it could have shared with the straight side of the land of light. So if someone takes that away and makes the straight crooked, so that what was in harmony now clashes and what fit together now recoils, would he remove any substance from it? Learn from this, then, that evil is not a substance. In a body, when its form changes for the worse, its form is lost or rather diminished, and what was previously called beautiful is called ugly, and a body that previously pleased now displeases. So in the soul, the honor of a right will—by which one lives piously and justly—is made crooked when the will changes for the worse. By that sin the soul becomes miserable, though it held blessedness through the honor of a right will, with no substance added or taken away.

Next, consider this too: even if we grant that for other reasons the side of the land of darkness is evil—because it is dark, because it is shadowy, or whatever else can be said—it is not evil in the fact that it is straight. Just as I grant that there is something evil in its color, so you must grant that there is something good in its straightness. It is therefore sacrilege to alienate this good, however great it is, from God the artificer, from whom comes every good in any nature; unless we believe this, we go astray most ruinously. How then does Mani say that this land is the supreme evil, when in the straightness of its side I find a good of no small beauty, as far as body is concerned, and he wants it to be utterly alien from the almighty and best God? To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Can we find anyone else?

But that side was evil too, he says. Suppose it was evil: it would certainly be worse if it were not straight but distorted. How then is it the supreme evil, if something worse than it can be thought? Furthermore, there must be some good whose loss makes any thing worse. By losing straightness that side would become worse; therefore straightness, some good, is in it. And you will never tell me where it comes from unless you take refuge in him from whom we confess that all goods come, whether great or small. But let us now pass from the consideration of this side to other matters.

problems.quote: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods?
problems.source_quote: cui alii tribuendum sit nisi auctori bonorum omnium. non inueniamus?
problems.why: 'non inueniamus?' = 'shall we not find [him]?' is a separate rhetorical question; English merges it into the preceding sentence as 'if not to.'
problems.fix: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Shall we not find him?
problems.ruling: 'non inueniamus?' omitted as standalone question; rhetorical structure lost, reader misled.

edits.old: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods?
edits.new: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Shall we not find him?

fixed: The source has 'cui alii tribuendum sit nisi auctori bonorum omnium. non inueniamus?' The 'non inueniamus?' is a separate rhetorical question meaning 'shall we not find [him]?', which the English merged into the preceding sentence. Added it as a separate question.

problems.why: Rhetorical question expects negative answer ('we shall not find [anyone else]'); English loses the force of 'we will not find [another]'
problems.fix: Shall we find anyone else? [We shall not.]

problems.quote: So that error may come to an end, let us simply work toward this: that at some point it may be finished.
problems.source_quote: ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur.
problems.why: careret is subjunctive 'that they might be free from errors'; object is the souls, not 'error' itself.
problems.fix: that they may be free from errors, let us simply work toward this: that at some point they may come to an end.
problems.ruling: careret is 3rd person imperfect subjunctive 'they might be free'; ut aliquando finiantur has subject 'they' (souls/people), not 'error'

problems.quote: It is therefore sacrilege to alienate this good, however great it is, from God the artificer—unless we believe that every good in any nature comes from him, we go astray most ruinously.
problems.source_quote: nefas est itaque hoc quantumcumque boni est alienare ab artifice deo, a quo esse omne bonum, quod in quacumque natura est, nisi credimus, perniciosissime erramus.
problems.why: The Latin means 'unless we believe that every good in any nature comes from him, we go astray most ruinously.' The dash breaks the sentence so 'unless we believe' seems to modify 'sacrilege' instead of 'erramus.'
problems.fix: It is therefore sacrilege to alienate this good, however great it is, from God the artificer, from whom comes every good in any nature; unless we believe this, we go astray most ruinously.
problems.ruling: Dash misstructures: nisi credimus belongs with perniciosissime erramus, not with nefas est; 'unless we believe' should modify 'we go astray'

edits.new: Shall we find anyone else? We shall not.

edits.old: So that error may come to an end, let us simply work toward this: that at some point it may be finished.
edits.new: So that they may be free from errors, let us simply work toward this: that at some point they may come to an end.

edits.new: It is therefore sacrilege to alienate this good, however great it is, from God the artificer, from whom comes every good in any nature; unless we believe this, we go astray most ruinously.

fixed: Omission: 'non inueniamus?' is a rhetorical question expecting a negative answer; the English 'Shall we not find him?' lost the force. Fixed to 'Shall we find anyone else? We shall not.'
Mistranslation: 'ut careret erroribus' refers to the souls being free from errors, not error coming to an end. Fixed to 'So that they may be free from errors...'

Mistranslation: The dash broke the sentence so 'unless we believe' seemed to modify 'sacrilege' instead of 'erramus.' Fixed to '...from whom comes every good in any nature; unless we believe this, we go astray most ruinously.'

problems.quote: So that they may be free from errors, let us simply work toward this: that at some point they may come to an end.
problems.source_quote: ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur
problems.why: 'careret' is singular; Augustine prays the person addressed may be free, not 'they'. 'finiantur' refers to the errors, not the person.
problems.fix: that he may be free from errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
problems.ruling: 'careret' singular subjunctive refers to one person (likely Mani/Fortunatus); 'finiantur' refers to errors ending, not persons. English misidentifies agency and antecedent.

problems.quote: would he not take away some of its beauty?
problems.why: Latin asks if he would take away NO beauty (nullamne), not 'some' beauty; rhetorical force differs.
problems.fix: would he not take away all its beauty?
problems.ruling: 'nullamne...pulchritudinem' asks 'would he take away NO beauty?' English 'some' inverts the rhetorical question's force.

problems.quote: Shall we find anyone else? We shall not.
problems.why: Latin is a question expecting 'no' (shall we not find?), not a confident 'We shall not'; English adds certainty source lacks.
problems.fix: Shall we not find anyone else?
problems.ruling: 'non inueniamus?' means 'shall we not find [anyone else]?' English 'Shall we find anyone else? We shall not' splits one question into statement, altering structure.

problems.quote: But that side was evil too, he says.
problems.source_quote: sed malum erat, inquit, etiam illud latus
problems.why: English omits 'inquit' marker, blurring that this is Mani speaking; speaker attribution lost.
problems.fix: But that side was evil too, he says.
problems.ruling: Source 'inquit' marks Mani as speaker; English 'he says' lacks it, losing speaker attribution in a debate context.

edits.new: So that he may be free from errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.

Mistranslation: 'nullamne' asks if he would take away NO beauty, not 'some'; edited to 'all its beauty'.

problems.quote: except the one who has not experienced God's mercy. That mercy is what frees a person from errors. Now, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
problems.source_quote: nisi qui diuinam misericordiam expertus non est. ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur.
problems.why: ut careret erroribus qualifies the mercy he has not received; it is not a new claim that mercy frees. The next clause only urges that the errors end.
problems.fix: except one who has not experienced God's mercy so as to be free from errors. Let us only work so that they may at some point come to an end.
problems.ruling: "ut careret erroribus" is a purpose/qualifier clause tied to the mercy; English invents "That mercy is what frees a person from errors" as a separate claim and loses the syntax; "tantum id agamus" is also misconstrued.

edits.old: except the one who has not experienced God's mercy. That mercy is what frees a person from errors. Now, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
edits.new: except the one who has not experienced God's mercy so as to be free from errors. Let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.

fixed: Fixed mercy/errors clause: source 'nisi qui diuinam misericordiam expertus non est. ut careret erroribus' makes 'ut careret' qualify the mercy not received; removed separate mercy-frees claim.

problems.quote: no one is mocking your past errors—except the one who has not experienced God's mercy so as to be free from errors. Let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
problems.source_quote: ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur.
problems.why: The 'ut careret erroribus' clause is a purpose clause attached to the previous sentence (the one without mercy, who doesn't wish to be free of errors); 'they' for errors is fine, but the clauses are muddled.
problems.fix: …except one who has not experienced God's mercy. To be rid of errors, let us only strive that they may at last come to an end.

edits.old: no one is mocking your past errors—except the one who has not experienced God's mercy so as to be free from errors. Let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
edits.new: no one is mocking your past errors—except the one who has not experienced God's mercy. To be rid of errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.

fixed: Fixed muddled clauses: respected period after 'expertus non est' and read 'ut careret erroribus' forward with 'tantum id agamus' as purpose, not as result of experiencing mercy.

fixed.quote: So that he may be free from errors
fixed.fix: That mercy is what frees a person from errors. Now
fixed.note: 'ut careret erroribus' belongs with the man who has not experienced the mercy that frees from error; it is not the goal of 'tantum id agamus', and 'he' points to nobody.

fixed.quote: would he not take away all its beauty
fixed.fix: would he not take away some of its beauty
fixed.note: 'nullamne ... pulchritudinem adimeret' asks whether he would take away any beauty at all; 'all its beauty' overstates it, and the proposed wording is awkward.

fixed.quote: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Shall we not find anyone else?
fixed.fix: To whom else should we attribute that very good which we find in it, if not to the author of all goods? Can we find anyone else?
fixed.note: Same problem as #1: the closing question must expect the answer 'no one else'; the proposed 'Shall we not find him?' does not match the Latin.

dismissed.why: 'nolitis' is 'you are unwilling,' not 'you want to'; 'unless you want to bark' reverses the sense to 'unless you refuse to bark.'
dismissed.note: 'si latrare nolitis' (if you do not want to bark) means the same as 'unless you want to bark'; the checker reversed the sense.

dismissed.why: 'obtinebat' is imperfect 'was holding/held,' but 'though' makes it concessive; Latin is explanatory/causal, not concessive.
dismissed.note: 'Though it held blessedness' fairly states the contrast between the soul's earlier blessed state and its present misery.

refereed.quote: To be rid of errors, let us work only toward this: that they may at some point come to an end.
refereed.source_quote: ut careret erroribus, tantum id agamus, ut aliquando finiantur.
refereed.why: Source: 'that he may be free of errors' (the one who lacks errors); English garbles the purpose clause, losing the point that the goal is the person's freedom from error.
refereed.fix: So that one may be free of errors, let us work only for this: that they may at some point come to an end.
refereed.ruling: ut careret is 3sg (that he lack errors); English folds it into finiantur and drops that person.
